# Axum vs Actix-web: Routing & Middleware (from README evidence)

## Sources
- **tokio-rs/axum**: [https://github.com/tokio-rs/axum](https://github.com/tokio-rs/axum) (27,326 stars, MIT)
- **actix/actix-web**: [https://github.com/actix/actix-web](https://github.com/actix/actix-web) (24,849 stars, Apache-2.0)

## Routing

| | **Axum** | **Actix-web** |
|---|---|---|
| Style | Macro-free API using `routing::{get, post}` combinators + `Router` builder | Powerful request routing with **optional macros** (`#[get("/hello/{name}")]`) |
| Example (README) | `.route("/", get(root)).route("/users", post(create_user))` | `#[get("/hello/{name}")]\nasync fn greet(name: web::Path<String>) -> impl Responder { … }` |
| Philosophy | Emphasizes "macro free API" and declarative request parsing via **extractors** | Supports both macro and non-macro dispatch via `App::new().service(...)` |

Axum's README explicitly highlights "Route requests to handlers with a macro free API" and declarative parsing via extractors as a high-level feature. Actix-web calls out "Powerful request routing with optional macros" in its Features section.

## Middleware

| | **Axum** | **Actix-web** |
|---|---|---|
| System | **Uses `tower::Service`** — no own middleware system | Built-in **Middlewares** (Logger, Session, CORS, etc.) |
| Ecosystem | Leverages the full [`tower`] and [`tower-http`] ecosystem; timeouts, tracing, compression, authorization "for free" | Provides middleware list directly; links to `/docs/middleware/` |
| Interop | Shares middleware with apps written using [`hyper`] or [`tonic`] | Integrates with `awc` HTTP client |

Axum's README explicitly states: *"axum doesn't have its own middleware system but instead uses `tower::Service`. This means axum gets timeouts, tracing, compression, authorization, and more, for free. It also enables you to share middleware with applications written using `hyper` or `tonic`."*

## Key takeaway (evidence-based)
- **Routing**: Axum favors a combinatorial, macro-free `Router` builder with extractors; Actix-web offers a powerful router with optional declarative macros.
- **Middleware**: Axum delegates entirely to the `tower::Service` ecosystem (reuse across hyper/tonic); Actix-web bundles its own middleware set (Logger, Session, CORS, etc.).

Both repos are built on Tokio and target high performance; Axum positions itself as a thin layer over `hyper`, while Actix-web claims one of the fastest frameworks per TechEmpower benchmarks.

## Reqwest `ClientBuilder` Timeout: Total Request vs Connect Timeout (with rustls)

### The three timeout methods

Reqwest's `ClientBuilder` exposes three distinct timeout settings that cover different phases of an HTTP request. Below is the definitive documentation (all sourced from the latest `docs.rs/reqwest`).

### 1. `timeout()` — total request deadline

> "Enables a total request timeout. The timeout is applied from when the request starts connecting until the response body has finished. Also considered a total deadline. Default is no timeout."
> — [docs.rs/reqwest/latest/reqwest/struct.ClientBuilder.html#method.timeout](https://docs.rs/reqwest/latest/reqwest/struct.ClientBuilder.html#method.timeout)

This is a **wall-clock deadline for the entire request**: DNS resolution + TCP connect + TLS handshake (including rustls certificate verification and key exchange) + sending the request body + waiting for response headers + streaming the response body. If any single phase exceeds the remaining budget, the request fails with a timeout error.

### 2. `connect_timeout()` — TCP/TLS connection phase only

> "Set a timeout for only the connect phase of a Client. Default is `None`. Note: This requires the futures be executed in a tokio runtime with a tokio timer enabled."
> — [docs.rs/reqwest/latest/reqwest/struct.ClientBuilder.html#method.connect_timeout](https://docs.rs/reqwest/latest/reqwest/struct.ClientBuilder.html#method.connect_timeout)

This covers **only the connection establishment**: TCP handshake + TLS handshake (rustls). It does NOT cover reading the response body. This is what you set when you want to fail fast on a stalled TCP/TLS negotiation without affecting the rest of the request.

### 3. `read_timeout()` — per-read stall detection

> "Enables a read timeout. The timeout applies to each read operation, and resets after a successful read. This is more appropriate for detecting stalled connections when the size isn't known beforehand. Default is no timeout."
> — [docs.rs/reqwest/latest/reqwest/struct.ClientBuilder.html#method.read_timeout](https://docs.rs/reqwest/latest/reqwest/struct.ClientBuilder.html#method.read_timeout)

This resets after every successful read and is useful for detecting a stalled response stream, not the overall request.

### Relationship diagram

```
request.start()
   │
   ├─ connect_timeout ──┐  (TCP + TLS/rustls handshake)
   │                    │
   ├─ read_timeout ─────┤  (per-read, resets after each read)
   │                    │
   └─ timeout (total) ──┘  (connect + read + body streaming)
```

### Practical example with rustls

Since reqwest v0.13, **rustls is the default TLS backend** [seanmonstar.com/blog/reqwest-v013-rustls-default](https://seanmonstar.com/blog/reqwest-v013-rustls-default/), so these timeouts govern rustls connections automatically. A typical configuration:

```rust
use std::time::Duration;

let client = reqwest::Client::builder()
    .timeout(Duration::from_secs(30))          // total deadline
    .connect_timeout(Duration::from_secs(5))   // TCP + TLS only
    .build()?;
```

### Key behavior notes

- If **only** `timeout()` is set (default `connect_timeout` is `None`), the total deadline still covers the connect phase — but you lose the ability to fail fast on a slow TCP/TLS handshake separately from a slow response body.
- The blocking `ClientBuilder` (feature `blocking`) has a **30-second default** for `timeout()`, while the async version defaults to `None` [docs.rs/reqwest/latest/reqwest/blocking/struct.ClientBuilder.html](https://docs.rs/reqwest/latest/reqwest/blocking/struct.ClientBuilder.html).
- `connect_timeout` requires a tokio runtime with a timer enabled [docs.rs/reqwest/latest/reqwest/struct.ClientBuilder.html#method.connect_timeout](https://docs.rs/reqwest/latest/reqwest/struct.ClientBuilder.html#method.connect_timeout).

### Summary

| Method | Scope | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `timeout()` | Connect + read + body (total deadline) | `None` (async), 30s (blocking) |
| `connect_timeout()` | TCP + TLS handshake only | `None` |
| `read_timeout()` | Per-read on response body | `None` |

The presence of rustls as the default TLS backend means the TLS handshake is part of **both** `connect_timeout` and `timeout`, so setting both avoids a slow rustls certificate verification from consuming the entire total deadline before any HTTP data is sent.
